title: Algorithms · Phase 3 · Optimisation
outline:
Phase 3 video (Algorithms, ECM3428 'Algorithms that Changed the World'): 'Optimisation: how to find the best answer'. 10 scenes, 117 s: title (4), the feasible region (12), the best point is a corner (12), simplex walk (15), bisection on the slope (12), golden section (13), Brent's parabola (13), Nelder-Mead moves (14), Nelder-Mead in a curved valley (13), recap (9). LESSONS (js/content/algo/algo-p3-*.js, all lecture 3, ids a3-*): a3-lp 3.1 (feasible region, slide the profit line, corners), a3-simplex 3.2 (enter, ratio test, stop), a3-bracket 3.3 (golden section, renumbered 3.12), a3-nm 3.4 (Nelder-Mead, renumbered 3.14); extras a3-formulate, a3-standard, a3-slack, a3-bakery, a3-implement, a3-apps, a3-convex 3.10 (one bowl), a3-bisect 3.11, a3-brent 3.13, a3-nm-ops 3.15, a3-nm-stop 3.16 and workshop a3-lab. Not shown (too detailed for 2 minutes): standard and slack form, the bakery example, the program, applications, convexity tests, Nelder-Mead stopping rules (only the end of scene 9 touches them).

STORY: optimisation = choose numbers to make a score as good as possible. (1) Linear programs: maximise z = 3x + 2y with rules x + 2y <= 10 (machine hours), 3x + y <= 15 (raw material), x, y >= 0. Each rule cuts the plane in half; the legal plans form the polygon with corners (0,0), (5,0), (4,3), (0,5). The lesson's five test plans: (2,2) legal, (4,3) legal (on both lines), (5,3) breaks both, (1,5) breaks the machine rule (11 > 10), (6,1) breaks the material rule (19 > 15). (2) Plans with equal z lie on a line 3x + 2y = z; sliding it outwards, the last touch is the corner (4,3) with z = 18; corner scores 0, 15, 18, 10, so only corners need checking. (3) Simplex walks edges: at (0,0) gains x +3, y +2 so x enters; ratio test machine 10, material 5 so material leaves; at (5,0), z 15, gains y +1 and slack s2 -1 so y enters; ratio test 3 (machine) and 15 (y-axis): machine leaves; at (4,3) the gains are -3/5 and -4/5: optimal, z 18. (4) One variable, no formula: for f(x) = e^x - 2x the slope is falling left of ln 2 = 0.6931 and rising right of it; bracket [0, 1] (f' = -1 and +0.718), bisect on the slope: m 0.5 (falling), 0.75 (rising), 0.625 (falling), 0.6875 (falling): width 1 -> 0.0625, bracket [0.6875, 0.75]. (5) Golden section on f(x) = 2.2 |x - 0.62|^1.4 + 0.25: a bracket is a triple with the lowest point in the middle, (0, 0.382, 1); one new probe per step (0.618, 0.764, 0.528, 0.674), widths 0.618, 0.382, 0.236, 0.146, 7 evaluations after 4 steps. (6) Brent on the same curve: parabola through the triple, jump to its bottom: 0.6067, 0.6408, 0.6116, then an unsafe jump (vertex 0.6207, step not shrinking) replaced by a golden probe 0.6228: bracket 0.029 wide after the same 7 evaluations (golden: 0.146). (7) Nelder-Mead: triangle B, G, W; reflect W through the centroid C; expand when R beats the best, contract when R overshoots, shrink as a last resort; example f = (x - 3.5)^2 + (y - 2.2)^2 from (0,0), (1,0), (0,1): expand, expand, reflect (expansion failed), contract inside. (8) Rosenbrock's valley from (-1, 1): 84 rounds, 198 evaluations, 29 reflect, 19 expand, 36 contract, 0 shrink, ends at (1, 1).

VIDEO-WIDE CONVENTIONS: COLOUR ROLES (whole video): green = allowed / better / kept / the answer; red = not allowed / worse / thrown away; blue = the point we look at (current corner, a probe, the triangle's middle corner); purple = the rules and the operators (constraint lines, the parabola, flip / stretch arrows and their candidate points); orange = the goal and the chosen (profit line, optimum star, entering variable, the minimum); grey = neutral (curves, grid, contours, unlit chips). Plots are grey and calm: curves and contours grey, 6 px curves, grey fill under a curve, the optimum / minimum is an orange star that only appears once found. Scenes 2-4 (LP) share the polygon with the same corner coordinates; scenes 5-7 (one variable) share the curve style, the bracket bar (P.span) under the axis, the red band for the thrown-away part and the stat cards (evaluations, width) at the top right; scenes 8-9 (Nelder-Mead) share the triangle (corner tones by rank: green best B, blue good G, red worst W; purple outline and purple candidate points R, E, M1, M2) and the four move chips (reflect purple, expand green, contract orange, shrink red). Tick and cross badges say 'better / not allowed' wherever a candidate is judged. The title card shows Byte (the Algorithms mascot).

title: Rules cut the plane,
what is left is legal
caps: Each rule is a line that cuts the plane in half.
Only the overlap passes both rules.
Plug a plan into every rule.
Pass them all and it is legal.
scenes.spec:
COLOUR ROLES (whole video): green = allowed / better / kept / the answer; red = not allowed / worse / thrown away; blue = the point we look at (current corner, a probe, the triangle's middle corner); purple = the rules and the operators (constraint lines, the parabola, flip / stretch arrows and their candidate points); orange = the goal and the chosen (profit line, optimum star, entering variable, the minimum); grey = neutral (curves, grid, contours, unlit chips).

IDEA: a linear program in one picture. We choose two numbers, x = units of product X and y = units of product Y. Each rule is a straight line that cuts the plane in half (one side is allowed). A plan is legal only if it passes EVERY rule, so the legal plans are the overlap of all the allowed sides: a polygon, the feasible region. Then test the lesson's five candidate plans against the rules.

title: Slide the profit line
until it leaves
caps: Each plan earns a score: z = 3x + 2y.
Slide the profit line outwards until it leaves.
It leaves at a corner, so check only the corners.
scenes.spec:
COLOUR ROLES (whole video): green = allowed / better / kept / the answer; red = not allowed / worse / thrown away; blue = the point we look at (current corner, a probe, the triangle's middle corner); purple = the rules and the operators (constraint lines, the parabola, flip / stretch arrows and their candidate points); orange = the goal and the chosen (profit line, optimum star, entering variable, the minimum); grey = neutral (curves, grid, contours, unlit chips).

IDEA: every plan earns a profit score z = 3x + 2y. All plans with the same z lie on one straight line. Slide that line outwards (z grows, the line stays parallel) until it is about to leave the polygon: the last point it touches is the optimum. A straight line can only leave a polygon at a corner, so the best plan is always a corner, and only the corners need checking. (Lesson a3-lp "Slide the profit line" and "Why a corner always wins".)

LAYOUT: the SAME plot call as scene 2 (P = A3.plot(stage, {x: 0, y: 0, w: 600, h: 604, view: [-0.6, 7.8, -0.6, 7.4], equal: true, axes: "origin", xticks: [0..7], yticks: [0..7], pad: {l: 60, r: 24, t: 24, b: 60}})), so the viewer sees the same picture. No red tints and no rule labels this time (keep it calm). title: Walk corner to corner,
never the middle
caps: Start at a corner. Which direction gains most?
Walk until the nearest rule blocks the way.
Repeat from the new corner.
No direction gains: the corner is optimal.
scenes.spec:
COLOUR ROLES (whole video): green = allowed / better / kept / the answer; red = not allowed / worse / thrown away; blue = the point we look at (current corner, a probe, the triangle's middle corner); purple = the rules and the operators (constraint lines, the parabola, flip / stretch arrows and their candidate points); orange = the goal and the chosen (profit line, optimum star, entering variable, the minimum); grey = neutral (curves, grid, contours, unlit chips).

IDEA: the simplex method never searches the inside. It stands on a corner and asks two questions: which direction gains most (the ENTERING variable, the largest gain per unit), and how far can I walk before a rule blocks me (the RATIO TEST, the smallest limit wins and that rule LEAVES). It walks to the next corner and repeats, and stops when no direction gains. On the lesson's LP it visits (0,0) -> (5,0) -> (4,3), never (0,5). (Lesson a3-simplex; the numbers come from A3.SIMPLEX, exact fractions.)

title: A slope that flips
traps the minimum
caps: Falling left, rising right: a minimum is trapped.
Test the middle: is the slope still falling?
Keep the half where the slope flips.
Each step halves the bracket.
scenes.spec:
COLOUR ROLES (whole video): green = allowed / better / kept / the answer; red = not allowed / worse / thrown away; blue = the point we look at (current corner, a probe, the triangle's middle corner); purple = the rules and the operators (constraint lines, the parabola, flip / stretch arrows and their candidate points); orange = the goal and the chosen (profit line, optimum star, entering variable, the minimum); grey = neutral (curves, grid, contours, unlit chips).

IDEA: when the minimum cannot be found by a formula, TRAP it. For a bowl-shaped function the slope is negative (falling) left of the bottom and positive (rising) right of it. If the slope is falling at a and rising at b, a minimum is trapped between them. Test the middle m: if the slope there is still falling, a moves up to m, otherwise b moves down to m; every cut keeps the guarantee and halves the bracket. (Lessons a3-bisect "From roots to minima", a3-convex; bisection on f' with f(x) = e^x - 2x, minimum at ln 2 = 0.6931.)

LAYOUT: P = A3.plot(stage, {x: 0, y: 0, w: 936, h: 560, view: [-0.2, 1.4, 0.45, 1.34], axes: "bottom", xticks: [0, 0.5, 1], grid: true, labels: false, pad: {l: 24, r: 24, t: 24, b: 80}}). curve = P.curve(A3.EXP.f, {x0: -0.2, x1: 1.4}) (grey, fillO 1). Handles: dots dA, dB = P.dot({tone: "blue", r: 14}), dM = P.dot({tone: "orange", r: 14}); three vertical guides P.vline({}) from the axis (y0 = P.cur.y0) up to the curve; letters P.text "a", "m", "b" at set({x, y: P.cur.y0, dy: -16}); three tangents tA, tB, tM = P.tangent({tone: "purple", len: 140}) with slope m = A3.EXP.df(x) at their point; three purple soft tags A3.tag(P.html, {anchor: "c", tone: "purple"}) reading "falling" or "rising", centred 60 px above their dot; band = P.band({tone: "red"}) (the thrown-away half); span = P.span({tone: "purple"}) (the bracket bar under the axis); width stat A3.stat(P.html, {x: 358, y: 24, w: 220, label: "bracket width"}); star = A3.star(P.over, {size: 52}).

DATA (A3.EXP and A3.bisect(4).rows, asserted): f(0) = 1, f(1) = 0.718, f'(0) = -1 falling, f'(1) = +0.718 rising, minimum f(ln 2) = 0.6137 at x = 0.6931. Rounds: 1) m = 0.5, slope -0.351 falling: a moves to 0.5, cut [0, 0.5], width 0.5. 2) m = 0.75, slope +0.117 rising: b moves to 0.75, cut [0.75, 1], width 0.25. 3) m = 0.625, slope -0.132 falling: a to 0.625, cut [0.5, 0.625], width 0.125. 4) m = 0.6875, slope -0.011 falling: a to 0.6875, cut [0.625, 0.6875], width 0.0625. Final bracket [0.6875, 0.75] contains ln 2. Use the rows' m, slope, falling, cut, wa, wb, width fields; slopes for the tangent = row.slope.

TIMELINE (local s):

title: No slope needed:
one new probe a step
caps: No slope? Three points can still trap a minimum.
Add one probe a step. The lowest stays in the middle.
Old probes are reused, so each cut costs one test.

title: Fit a parabola,
jump to its bottom
caps: Same curve. Fit a parabola through the three points.
Jump to the bottom of the parabola.

title: A triangle flips
its worst corner
caps: Keep a triangle. Flip its worst corner through the middle.
A great flip? Stretch even further.
Stretched too far? Keep the plain flip.
Flip overshoots? Pull the corner in instead.
Nothing works? Shrink towards the best.

COLOUR ROLES (whole video): green = allowed / better / kept / the answer; red = not allowed / worse / thrown away; blue = the point we look at (current corner, a probe, the triangle's middle corner); purple = the rules and the operators (constraint lines, the parabola, flip / stretch arrows and their candidate points); orange = the goal and the chosen (profit line, optimum star, entering variable, the minimum); grey = neutral (curves, grid, contours, unlit chips).

IDEA: Nelder-Mead needs no gradient and no formula, only the VALUES of f. In 2-D it keeps a triangle of three points, sorted into best B, good G and worst W. Each round it replaces W: flip it through the middle C of the best side (reflect: R). A great flip (R beats the best) earns a longer try (expand: E, kept if better than R). A flip that is no better than G overshot: try the two points halfway towards C (contract: M1 inside, M2 outside, the better one wins if it beats W). If nothing works, shrink everything halfway towards B. Good news earns a bigger move, bad news a smaller one. (Lessons a3-nm, a3-nm-ops; example from the lesson's runner: f = (x - 3.5)^2 + (y - 2.2)^2, minimum 0 at (3.5, 2.2), start triangle (0,0), (1,0), (0,1).)

title: It crawls down
a curved valley
caps: Real problems have curved valleys, not simple bowls.
The triangle stretches along the valley.
Near the bottom it shrinks to a tiny triangle.
No derivatives needed, just comparisons.
scenes.spec:
COLOUR ROLES (whole video): green = allowed / better / kept / the answer; red = not allowed / worse / thrown away; blue = the point we look at (current corner, a probe, the triangle's middle corner); purple = the rules and the operators (constraint lines, the parabola, flip / stretch arrows and their candidate points); orange = the goal and the chosen (profit line, optimum star, entering variable, the minimum); grey = neutral (curves, grid, contours, unlit chips).

IDEA: the payoff. On a curved valley (Rosenbrock's banana, f(x, y) = 100 (y - x^2)^2 + (1 - x)^2, minimum 0 at (1, 1)) a fixed-size step would bang into the walls. Nelder-Mead's triangle changes shape: it stretches along the valley when moves work, squeezes when they do not, and ends as a tiny triangle on the minimum, using only comparisons. The real run of the lesson (a3-nm-stop): start x0 = (-1, 1) with two 10 % nudges, stop when the triangle and its values are within 1e-6.

A. DATA AND ALGORITHMS (common.js, common-2.js; each result is asserted against the numbers in the scene specs, a mismatch throws "VID.a3: ..."):
 LP: A3.LP, A3.CORNERS [[0,0],[5,0],[4,3],[0,5]], A3.CORNER_Z [0,15,18,10], A3.BEST [4,3], A3.PLANS, A3.z(p), A3.check(p) -> {m, r, okM, okR, ok}, A3.iso(z), A3.clip(poly, a, b, r).
 SIMPLEX: A3.SIMPLEX = {steps: [{from, z, nb, gains (fractions {n, d}), enter, ratios: [{row, val}], leave, to, zTo}], final: {at, z, nb, gains}}; A3.qv(q) -> number, A3.qt(q) -> "−3/5"; A3.ROW_NAME {s1: machine, s2: material, x: y-axis, y: x-axis}.
 BISECTION (slope of f(x) = e^x - 2x): A3.EXP {f, df, min}; A3.bisect(n) -> {rows: [{k, a, b, m, slope, falling, keep, cut, width, wa, wb}], a, b}.
 GOLDEN / BRENT (f = A3.BF, kinked dip, minimum 0.25 at 0.62): A3.golden(n) and A3.brent(n) -> {start, steps: [{k, t, x, fx, nt, cut, width, evals, (golden: lower), (brent: kind "P"|"G", why, vertex, step)}]} with triples {a, b, c, fa, fb, fc}; A3.parab(t), A3.lagrange(t) (the parabola as a function), A3.goldenX, A3.retriple; zoom helpers A3.viewFor(t, {padX, y0, y1, top}) and A3.mixView(v0, v1, k).
 NELDER-MEAD: A3.BOWL2, A3.ROSEN, A3.nmIter, A3.nmRun(f, pts, {n, stop}) -> {rounds, slots, best, centre, evAt, counts, ev, it, final}; A3.NM_BOWL (4 rounds, scene 8), A3.NM_ROS (84 rounds, scene 9); A3.nmAt(run, u) -> {slots, best, centre, trail, centreTrail, counts, it, frac} (u = fractional round, corners move smoothly, a surviving corner keeps its slot); A3.nmShrink(sortedTriangle) -> {B, G, W}; A3.contours(f, view, levels, {n, log}) -> level segments (data coords) with A3.BOWL_LEVELS and A3.ROS_LEVELS.
 SMALL: A3.fmt(v, digits) (real minus), A3.rng(seed), A3.need(ok, msg), A3.near / near2.

B. DRAWING. Create handles once in build(); in update(t) call .set({...}) on EVERY handle with the full state (anything left out falls back to its default; nothing is remembered). Opacity o, draw-on k, pop s (use V.ease.pop), dx / dy in stage px (dy > 0 is down).
 A3.plot(parent, {x, y, w, h, view: [x0, x1, y0, y1], equal, pad, frame, grid, xticks, yticks, labels, axes: "origin" | "bottom" | "none", clip}) -> P with P.px / P.py / P.pt (data -> stage px), P.view(v) (animate the window: call it first in update), P.set({o, s, dy}), P.under / P.mid / P.over (SVG layers in stage px), P.html (HTML layer for tags). Handles: P.curve(fn, {tone, w, x0, x1, base}).set({k, o, tone, w, fillO, fn}); P.eq(a, b, r).set({k, o, tone, rev, r}) (line a x + b y = r, clipped to the window; r can slide); P.half(a, b, r).set({o}) (tints the side a x + b y >= r); P.poly().set({pts, o, fillO, strokeO, tone}); P.path().set({pts, o, k, tone}) (open polyline); P.dot({tone, r}).set({x, y, o, s, tone, dx, dy, ring, ringK}); P.ring({r}).set({x, y, r, o, tone}); P.text({fs, tone, anchor, px}).set({text, x, y, dx, dy, o, tone, s, r}) (y is the baseline; paper halo); P.vline().set({x, y0, y1, o, k, tone}); P.band().set({x0, x1, o, tone}); P.span().set({x0, x1, o, tone}) (bracket bar under the axis); P.tangent().set({x, y, m, o, k, tone, len}); P.arrow().set({x1, y1, x2, y2, k, o, tone, bow}); P.contours(levels).set({o, tone}); P.simplex().set({pts, tones, labels, o, fillO, ring, dotO}).
 Stickers (HTML, pass the stage or P.html): A3.tag(parent, {x, y, text, tone, solid, fs, anchor: "l"|"c"|"r"|"m"}) -> el.set({text, html, tone, solid, s, o, dx, dy, r}); A3.chip(parent, {x, y, w, h, text, tone}).set({state: "grey"|"active"|"done", pop, o, dx, dy, pulse, text}); A3.sticker(parent, {x, y, w, h, text, tone, icon: "tick"|"cross"}).set({text, tone, icon, k, o, dx, dy}); A3.badge(parent, {x, y (centre), size, icon, text, tone}).set({icon, text, tone, k, o, x, y, dx, dy, s}); A3.stat(parent, {x, y, w, h, label, tone}).set({text, o, bump, tone, dx, dy, s}); A3.bars(parent, {x, y, w, rows, min, max, labelW, valW, title, ...}).set({vals, k, tones, texts, labels, hi, rowO, o, dy}) (signed bars supported, B.h = card height); A3.moves(parent, {x, y, w, h}).set({active, used, counts, pop, o, pulse}) (the four Nelder-Mead chips); A3.star(parent, {size}) and A3.diamond(parent, {size}) -> .set({x, y, s, o, r, dx, dy}) (parent: an SVG element such as P.over, or an HTML element).
 Reused from l5: VID.l5.tone(name) -> CSS var names, VID.l5.tick / cross / arrow / drawOn, VID.l5.svg(parent).
